episode_title: Can We Build Switzerland in India?

stories.topic: The Tourist Who Comes After Me
stories.summary: Reflecting on the bittersweet end of the Bir Sessions, Amit notes how places he once loved on vacation eventually get crowded and touristy. He concedes the irony with a quip: 'the definition of too many tourists is the tourist who comes after me.' We always want the place pristine for ourselves but spoiled the moment someone arrives behind us.
stories.insight: A tidy diagnosis of the hypocrisy at the heart of tourism complaints. The honest version of 'this place is ruined' is almost always 'this place is ruined for me' — useful for separating genuine sustainability arguments from mere territorialism.

stories.summary: At an Everything is Everything viewers' meetup in Bir, a young man named Shubham Dhiman drove three hours from a village near Hamirpur. He had done the Takshashila public policy course, was full of curiosity, and told Ajay he didn't want to leave for the city — he wanted to do something for Himachal. His conversation with Ajay sparked the framing for the entire episode on Himalayan development.
stories.insight: Rooted local talent — people who know a place and refuse to leave it — is the actual scarce input for sustainable development. The episode is partly a letter to Shubham: here is the toolkit for the work you've chosen.

stories.topic: How Udaipur Saved Itself By Reprioritising Water
stories.summary: Udaipur's lakes used to be hit-and-miss — beautiful in good monsoon years, dry in bad ones, with tourists cancelling because 'the lake's empty.' Vasundhara Raje, Rajiv Mehrishi and others changed Rajasthan's irrigation rules so that, no matter the scarcity, Udaipur's lakes got water first, before agriculture. Tourism returned, GDP soared, and an entire service economy grew around the city — making Udaipur one of the most beautiful cities in the world.
stories.insight: A textbook case of how a single, deliberate trade-off — informed by basic economic logic about which sector creates more value per drop of water — can change a region's destiny. Sustainable tourism isn't an accident; it's policy.

stories.topic: Three Thousand Abandoned Villages In Uttarakhand
stories.summary: Ajay describes hiking up to Panchachuli and finding villages with 200 houses but only three families left — hikers were told they could each take a whole abandoned house for the night. There are over 3,000 such abandoned villages in Uttarakhand. He recalls another anecdote from the Pindari Glacier trek: a pregnant woman had to be carried 20 km on a stretcher by four men to reach a health facility. People are migrating out for entirely rational reasons.
stories.insight: The standard 'population pressure on Himalayan ecosystems' framing is decades out of date. The demographic transition has flipped — the Himalayan states now face quiet depopulation, not Malthusian pressure, which fundamentally changes what policy needs to do.

stories.topic: An Abandoned Village In The Sahyadris
stories.summary: On a nine-day trek in January where Ajay broke his ankle on day five, day three brought him to a modest Sahyadri village of about twenty houses with exactly one old man and one old woman ('a Matara and a Matari') still living there. Everyone else had left.
stories.insight: The depopulation story isn't just Himalayan — it's spreading. Outward migration from remote rural India is a national phenomenon and a structural condition that any place-based policy now has to start from.

stories.topic: The Slow Death Of Dharamshala (And McLeod Ganj, And Lower Dharamkot, And Upper Dharamkot)
stories.summary: When the Dalai Lama arrived in 1959 and the airport opened around 1960, Dharamshala was beautiful. By the 1980s, urban governance had collapsed and it became 'a bad Indian city.' High-value tourists migrated up to McLeod Ganj — for about 20 years it worked, then it too went bad. Then to Lower Dharamkot, then to Upper Dharamkot. Now Dharamshala is a cricket stadium destination, and cricket brings low-value tourists. Ajay predicts Upper Dharamkot is next to be destroyed.
stories.insight: The Himalayan tourism failure isn't a single collapse — it's a recurring stair-step. Each time a place is degraded, the high-value cohort moves uphill, the low-value cohort fills in, the cycle restarts. Without urban governance, every charming village inherits its predecessor's death.

stories.topic: Standing At Billing, Looking Down At The Smoke
stories.summary: The day before recording, Ajay was at Billing at 2,500 metres looking down at Bir 800 metres below. The valley was a haze of solid particulate matter — visible bonfires lit by tourists ('the bad kinds of tourists'). The view was destroyed for everybody. He argues only the state, with drones and thermal cameras and ten-thousand-rupee fines, can fix this.
stories.insight: Air quality and view-quality are public goods; bonfires are textbook negative externalities. The 'libertarian by default' instinct misfires here: this is precisely the pure-market-failure case where the state has to act, because no individual will pay to stop another's bonfire.

stories.topic: Trek The Sahyadris Changed His Life At Eleven
stories.summary: At about age 11, Ajay walked into a book fair in Bombay and stumbled on Harish Kapadia's Trek The Sahyadris. He bought it, read it a hundred times, and with no knowledge or proper help started hiking the Sahyadris with a bunch of other kids from Patrakar Colony in Bandra East. He calls Kapadia a turning point in his life.
stories.insight: A single book, picked up by accident at the right age, can produce a lifelong relationship with the outdoors. The mechanism of this episode — write the book, plant the seed in the Shubhams of the world — is exactly how Ajay was made.

recommendations.creator: Alain Bertaud
recommendations.context: Bertaud's masterwork on urban planning and economics.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a desert-island book — not just on town planning but on how urban planning and economics come together to shape cities and human lives. Source of much of the episode's town-planning frame, including the principle that 40-50% of land must be drawn upfront on maps as streets and parks.

recommendations.creator: Barry Lopez
recommendations.context: Lopez's reflective book on travel, landscape, and the natural world.
recommendations.reason: Surrounded by Bir's beauty, Amit thought of Lopez — one of the great travel writers, a 'philosopher of the world.' Every journey, Amit notes, becomes truly beautiful only when it is also a journey inside us, and Lopez is the master of that double movement.

recommendations.creator: Harish Kapadia
recommendations.context: Kapadia's classic guide to hiking the Sahyadri range.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's life-changing book at age 11 — the volume that turned him into a hiker. He addresses the author directly: 'Harish Kapadia, you changed my life.'

recommendations.creator: Harish Kapadia
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it one of the lovely books and essential reading for anyone interested in the Himalayas — a continuation of the spell that Trek The Sahyadris cast on him decades earlier.

recommendations.creator: Malini Goyal and Prashanth Prakash
recommendations.context: A book on Bangalore's contradictions as a city.
recommendations.reason: Source of the line Amit uses to summarise the urban governance problem: 'In Bangalore the software is 5G but the hardware is 2G.' For Bir, he says, 'the software is the hardware' — which is why getting town planning right is non-negotiable.

recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with the journalist Malini Goyal.
recommendations.reason: Companion to Unboxing Bengaluru — the long-form conversation with Goyal about the Bangalore predicament that the chapter on hardware vs software sits inside.

recommendations.item: Pritika Hingorani Wants to Fix Our Cities (Episode 361, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pritika Hingorani
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Pritika Hingorani on urban governance.
recommendations.reason: Background reading for the episode's claim that the 'urban dreamers and town planners of India' should redirect attention from Bangalore and Bombay to smaller towns — Hingorani is one of the people Ajay names as the right kind of expertise to draw on.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the chapter title 'You Must Learn to Walk Before You Can Run' — the public-policy reasoning Ajay invokes for why Bir, not Bangalore, is the right place to try to get urban governance right.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous EIE episode on development.
recommendations.reason: Direct prequel — episode 57 lays the general development framework that this episode applies to the special case of Himalayan regions.

recommendations.item: India Needs Decentralization (Episode 47, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on the subsidiarity principle.
recommendations.reason: Background for this episode's premise that local political systems must drive the prioritisation of local problems — a direct application of the subsidiarity principle.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: Referenced when Ajay rules out an agriculture-led growth path for Himalayan states. The earlier episode lays out the case for market-based agriculture; the geography of the Himalayas means even that recipe doesn't work here.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode making the case against Malthusian framings of Indian population.
recommendations.reason: Connects to the demographic-transition argument here: India is now in a very different stage of the journey, and Himalayan states in particular are seeing fertility collapse and abandoned villages, not population pressure.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on the public-economics framework for state intervention.
recommendations.reason: The disciplined approach Ajay invokes here — start from freedom, identify market failures, only then ask what the state can usefully add — is the framework spelled out at length in episode 26.

recommendations.item: The Hiking Episode (Episode 35, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on hiking, with Ajay sharing his outdoors journey.
recommendations.reason: Amit recommends it at the close — 'what Harish Kapadia was to you, you could be for many young people' — pointing viewers toward Ajay's own hiking story as a way to seed the same passion in them.

core_ideas.concept: First Principles For Place: Loyalty Is To Local Livelihoods, Not Outsider Aesthetics
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay refuses the condescending outsider position — 'we want you to live at low income because your places are nicer for us.' The only legitimate goal of Himalayan policy is the sustained economic development of these regions for their own people. Aesthetics are downstream of livelihoods; the question is which strategy genuinely raises GDP per capita over a hundred-year horizon.
core_ideas.quote: Our only loyalty is to the sustained economic development of these regions in a way that caters to the welfare and the livelihoods of the people here.

core_ideas.concept: Coastlines Are Magic; The Himalayas Are Not (For Industry)
core_ideas.explanation: In development economics, coastlines are quasi-magical — they give frictionless access to container ships and the world economy. Himalayan states are landlocked and far from the coast, leaving them dependent on airports, railways and highways that are extraordinarily expensive to build and maintain in mountain terrain. Any pure-industrialisation strategy will always be roughly 50% inferior to plains-based industrialisation, condemning the region to permanent per-capita-GDP underperformance. So the standard recipe of factories-plus-modern-agriculture is structurally the wrong recipe for the Himalayas.
core_ideas.quote: If you just say I'm going to do normal industrialisation and agriculture, then in a way you're a bit doomed.

core_ideas.concept: Sell What You Have: The Himalayas As Singular Asset
core_ideas.explanation: The right Himalayan economic strategy starts from the fact that there is exactly one Himalayas on planet Earth. Switzerland, Colorado and Japan have all built first-world-quality lives around their natural beauty by selling the locale itself — high-value tourism is one of the world's most prosperous industries. The Himalayan playbook is to do likewise: build a high-end tourism economy that is sustainable across generations rather than a flash-in-the-pan boom-and-bust.
core_ideas.quote: Udaipur has its lakes and the Himalayan states have the Himalayas.

core_ideas.concept: The Demographic Transition Has Flipped The Problem
core_ideas.explanation: The old Malthusian framing — too many people for the Himalayan ecosystem to bear — is empirically obsolete. Total fertility rates across Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Bhutan are now 1.6-1.7. Combined with outward migration, populations are gently declining; over 3,000 villages in Uttarakhand are already abandoned. The policy environment is no longer 'how do we feed the masses?' but 'how do we build viable livelihoods for a shrinking, dispersed population?' — and tourism's relatively low labour-density is now an asset, not a problem.
core_ideas.quote: Those problems are largely behind us.

core_ideas.concept: Negative Externalities And The N x P Equation
core_ideas.explanation: Tourism GDP equals N (number of tourists) multiplied by P (per-day spend). Maximising N alone collapses P — you trade your high-spending visitors for a flood of low-spending ones, and the place becomes worse for both. The mechanism is negative externalities: each hotel rationally installs disco lights and 5,000-watt speakers to attract tourists, but each one destroys a 200-metre radius around it. Uncoordinated rational choices create collectively irrational ruin.
core_ideas.quote: They've just destroyed a circle with a radius of 200 metres surrounding themselves.

core_ideas.concept: The Stair-Step Death Of Indian Hill Stations
core_ideas.explanation: Mussoorie, Shimla, Nainital, Dharamshala — the same arc plays out over and over. A place is discovered, becomes great, gets overrun, urban governance fails, high-value tourists flee uphill to the next pristine spot, low-value tourism floods in, the place collapses into a stable equilibrium of poverty. The high-value cohort then repeats the move (Dharamshala -> McLeod Ganj -> Lower Dharamkot -> Upper Dharamkot). Each step is a 20-30 year bubble, then a slum. Without intervention, every charming Himalayan village is a hill station in waiting.
core_ideas.quote: You get brief growth, it goes away. You get brief growth, it goes away.

core_ideas.explanation: 'Sustainable' here is not an environmental aesthetic — it is a long-horizon economic concept. Switzerland, Colorado and the Japanese alps have first-world locals because they have managed to keep N x P high for generations, building human capital across a century-long arc. In India, the same arc keeps getting cut short at year 20-30 by negative externalities. The dream should be Bir as the Switzerland of India, but only if we recognise the timescale: building human capital is a hundred-year journey.
core_ideas.quote: It will take a hundred years to become Switzerland.

core_ideas.concept: The Walk-Before-You-Run Argument For Bir Over Bangalore
core_ideas.explanation: Bangalore, Bombay and Delhi seem hopeless cases for urban governance. The orthodox response is to keep grinding at them. Ajay reverses the priority: India's best urban planners (Bimal Patel, Pritika Hingorani, Janagraha) should redirect their attention to small towns like Bir. Two reasons. First, smaller problems are more tractable — learn here, scale later. Second, incentive compatibility: in Bangalore the product is software, so urban quality is a complaint people grumble about but can ignore. In Bir the product *is* the place — urban quality and GDP are the same variable, so political will aligns naturally with good governance.
core_ideas.quote: You must learn to walk before you can run.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay reframes Bangalore's urban dysfunction as a resource curse. Software firms keep generating wealth no matter how bad the city becomes; the state apparatus then becomes predatory, extracting from those firms instead of serving residents. By contrast, Udaipur's police force has internalised that one bad incident — a woman unsafe at 2 a.m., a tourist mistreated — costs the city millions. The feedback loop is tight, and policing improves accordingly. Tourism towns get better governance precisely because their revenue is held hostage to that governance.
core_ideas.quote: Somebody is making the software and there is a predatory state that tries to extract money from those people.

core_ideas.concept: Town Planning As Drawing Lines On Maps Early
core_ideas.explanation: Following Bimal Patel: the foundational act of urban planning is allocating roughly 40-50% of land to streets and parks, drawn on the map *before* unstructured construction takes over. Once buildings come up, you can never claw back the space. Bir today has one road and a paragliding landing zone and no other parks; the moment to draw the grid is now. This is *not* the micromanaging Indian style of planning ('here a school, here a petrol pump') — it's the lighter, foundational discipline of pre-allocating the public spaces that everything else will need.
core_ideas.quote: Once the unstructured construction comes, then there is no room to build the streets.

core_ideas.concept: Airports As Filters For High-Value Tourism
core_ideas.explanation: High-value tourists fly. Ladakh works as a high-value destination because the only realistic way in is to fly to Delhi and then to Leh — the activation energy of the trip self-selects for affluent, intentional visitors. Roads, by contrast, lower the bar and admit the low-value cohort. The policy implication for Himachal: build longer airport runways (Kangra is 1,300 m, Kullu is 1,100 m — too short for big aircraft), because the airport is a filter that engineers the tourist mix at the inlet.
core_ideas.quote: There is an activation energy, there is a bump that is required before a person will go to Ladakh.

core_ideas.concept: Parks Should Generate GDP, Not Just Preserve Biodiversity
core_ideas.explanation: Indian national parks today stop poaching and prevent commercial development — both good. They have not yet learned how to contribute to GDP. Yellowstone (~9,000 sq km) gets four million visitors a year spending $1,000-$2,000 each — $4-8 billion in revenue. India needs the same model for places like the Great Himalayan National Park: gateway villages on the border (Bir-style), hundreds of kilometres of internal walking trails, modest interior campgrounds and a small amount of high-end accommodation operated by private vendors under strict biodiversity contracts. Wildlife protection and high per-capita GDP are not inconsistent goals.

core_ideas.concept: Public Goods That Only The State Can Provide
core_ideas.explanation: Air quality across North India is the canonical example: no individual can stop another's bonfire; only the state, with drones, thermal cameras and ten-thousand-rupee fines, can fix particulate pollution. Similarly with noise, light pollution and solid waste management. These are the textbook market failures where the freedom-first public-economics framework licenses state action — and where Bir, currently breathing the smoke of tourist bonfires, urgently needs it.
core_ideas.quote: Only the state can fix air quality in North India.

core_ideas.explanation: Throughout the conversation, Ajay returns to a simple sequencing claim: action without knowledge produces yet another failed Indian project. Before doing anything in Bir, the people who care about it should connect to the right pockets of expertise — Bimal Patel for town planning, Janagraha for urban governance, the wildlife and parks community for ecosystem protection. Don't accept the default Indian way of doing town planning. Do the upfront work of learning what 'right' looks like, then pursue it with the locals' own incentive structure behind you.
core_ideas.quote: The knowledge comes first, the ideas come first.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's definition of overcrowding: 'The definition of too many tourists is the tourist who comes after me.'
Amit on the Indian-cinema-aside that started the show: 'Content milega. Content milega to the world.' — followed immediately by Ajay correcting himself, 'You don't say things like content milega.'
Ajay's image of unchecked Bir: '5,000 watts of amplification' and 'blinking lights so the aliens can see us from Alpha Centauri.'
Amit pre-emptively walking back the 'low-value tourist' framing: 'It sounds really snobbish — like, in hamare logon ko jo chahiye, these plebeians are spoiling it all.'

Amit's apology to the cricket fan watching: 'If there are any cricket people watching this, kindly excuse — we love you, I love you, we love cricket, all cricket people are not the same, we contain multitudes.'
Amit catching himself mid-soliloquy: 'I'm sounding like a pop philosopher. Enough of this.'
Ajay's promise to readers: 'If you ask us in triplicate, we will give you the latitude and longitude of the location where each session was recorded.'
Steven Pinker's frame, repeated from earlier episodes: 'Nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them' — extended here to argue that regions also have differing-size knobs.
John Maynard Keynes invoked as the patron saint of disciplined public economics — start from freedom, identify market failures, then ask what the state can uniquely add.
Dire Straits, 'Telegraph Road' from Love Over Gold — Ajay's musical accompaniment to the natural arc of a beautiful place being discovered, settled and overrun.

John Lennon's 'Watching the Wheels' and Bruce Springsteen's 'Everything Is Everything' — the two song titles Amit and Ajay considered for the show, decided on a lakeside in Udaipur a year before launch.
Bimal Patel's town-planning catechism: drawing 40-50% of land on the map upfront as streets and parks, before construction forecloses the option.

Yellowstone National Park as benchmark: ~9,000 sq km, four million tourists a year, $1,000-$2,000 spend per tourist, $4-8 billion in annual revenue — the model India's national parks have not yet matched.
Udaipur as 'the Venice of the East' — Ajay's framing for a city that traded B-grade agriculture for world-class tourism and won.
Malini Goyal's pithy line on Bangalore: 'The software is 5G but the hardware is 2G' — extended by Amit to Bir, where 'the software is the hardware.'
